explanation:
## The program

```cpp
bool by4{ year % 4 == 0 };
bool by100{ year % 100 == 0 };
bool by400{ year % 400 == 0 };

bool leap{ by4 && (!by100 || by400) };

std::cout << (leap ? "leap" : "common") << "\n";
```

## The brackets

`&&` has higher precedence than `||`, exactly as `*` has higher
precedence than `+`. So this:

```cpp
by4 && !by100 || by400
```

means `(by4 && !by100) || by400`, which says "a leap year is one
that divides by 4 but not 100, **or** anything divisible by 400".
That happens to be true of every year, because every year divisible
by 400 also divides by 4 — so the two rules agree on every input,
and the missing brackets do not show up as a wrong answer here at
all.

Which is the point worth taking away. Relying on precedence you have
to look up is a bet that the next person to edit the line will look
it up too. The brackets cost nothing and say what you meant.

## Why "unless" becomes an OR

```
not divisible by 100   OR   divisible by 400
```

reads as "the century exception does not apply to you, or it does
and you are excused from it". Rules with an exception to the
exception almost always come out as this shape: the general case,
`||` the escape.

The same thing written as nested `if`s is longer and no clearer:

```cpp
if (year % 4 != 0)        leap = false;
else if (year % 100 != 0) leap = true;
else if (year % 400 != 0) leap = false;
else                      leap = true;
```

It is correct, and it is four places to make a mistake instead of
one. Worth writing out once to convince yourself it says the same
thing.

## bool is a type, not just a condition

`year % 4 == 0` is an expression whose value is `true` or `false`,
and there is nothing special about storing it. Beginners often write

```cpp
if (year % 4 == 0) by4 = true; else by4 = false;
```

which is four extra words for `bool by4{ year % 4 == 0 };`. The
condition already **is** the answer.

## What this does not check

The calendar. The Gregorian rule was adopted in 1582 and different
countries switched at different times, so "was 1500 a leap year"
has no single answer. This problem is the arithmetic rule applied
uniformly, and says so in its constraints rather than pretending to
be a date library.
